A vector store is the component of a RAG system that makes retrieval fast.
Documents are split into chunks, each chunk is converted into a numeric
vector called an embedding, and the vectors are indexed so that, given a
new query vector, the system can quickly find the stored vectors that are
closest to it in the embedding space. Closeness in that space is meant to
correspond to closeness in meaning, so a nearest-neighbor search over
embeddings behaves like a semantic search over text.

Popular vector stores fall into two categories. Managed, cloud-hosted
databases such as Pinecone and Weaviate handle scaling, replication, and
filtering for production workloads. Lightweight, embeddable libraries such
as FAISS, developed by Meta, run inside a single process and are a common
choice for prototypes, research, and smaller applications because they add
no external infrastructure.

Most vector stores use an approximate nearest neighbor algorithm rather
than an exact search, because exact search over millions of high-dimensional
vectors is too slow for real-time queries. Approximate methods such as
HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs) trade a small amount of
recall for a very large speedup, which is usually the right trade-off for
interactive applications where a response is expected in under a second.
